source.version: Published journal article, Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 2026, 42(2), 39-59; DOI 10.14742/ajet.10564 (PDF pp. 1 and 21, title page and suggested citation).
source.title_on_document: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT on college students’ mathematical creativity: A quasi-experimental study

paper_design_summary: Yangzhou University student volunteers were explicitly reported as randomly assigned to ChatGPT-assisted or unassisted mathematical creativity tasks in controlled classroom sessions, despite the quasi-experimental label in the title (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure). The analyzed sample comprised 60 ChatGPT participants and 64 controls; ChatGPT participants received interaction training and structured prompts, while controls worked with traditional tools without support (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Figures 1-2, Procedure, and Participants). Two scorers coded the students’ solutions to four open-ended mathematical tasks for flexibility, fluency, and originality, aggregated at participant level (PDF pp. 8-10, printed pp. 46-48, MCT and Mathematical creativity scoring).

studies.label: ChatGPT assistance on mathematical creativity tasks

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were assigned to task resolution with ChatGPT or without ChatGPT. The methods explicitly state random assignment; the randomization procedure and allocation concealment are not described.
assignment.quote: All students were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (task resolution with ChatGPT) or the control group (task resolution without ChatGPT).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Methods, Procedure; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1.

arms.name: Experimental group (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students used ChatGPT on identical personal computers, received technical training and structured interaction prompts, and could iteratively refine responses while solving the tasks. Figure 1 labels this group N = 60, consistent with the retained sample in Table 2 (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Figures 1-2, Procedure, and Tables 1-2).

arms.name: Control group (without ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students used traditional tools such as paper and pencil and received no external support or prompts. Figure 1 labels this group N = 64, consistent with the retained sample in Table 2 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1 and Procedure; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Table 2).

participants.exclusions: Students who withdrew were not analyzed and their questionnaires were not collected; none of the collected questionnaires were subsequently excluded (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure). The number of withdrawals is not stated. Figure 1 gives group counts of 60 and 64 but does not distinguish initial assignment counts from the retained sample; randomized counts are therefore left null (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43).
participants.who: Student volunteers from all majors at Yangzhou University, recruited for course credits. The paper reports no specific mathematics background and similar prior mathematics course performance (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants).
participants.quote: Since no prior sample size calculation was performed, a sensitivity analysis was conducted based on the sample size (n = 124)
participants.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1 (experimental N = 60; control N = 64); PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Procedure, for recruitment and withdrawals.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, GPT-4o (interface label ChatGPT 4o in PDF p. 6, printed p. 44, Figure 2); exact model build not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Students entered prompts and refined replies while solving the mathematical creativity tasks, supported by interaction training and structured example, heuristic, task-reminder, critical-thinking, and divergent-thinking prompts. The model supplied ideas and prototypical solutions, so this was not a content-free coaching intervention. The model was fixed and interactions were logged (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure, Figures 1-2, and Table 1; PDF p. 14, printed p. 52, Discussion).

task.description: Four open-ended mathematical creativity tasks adapted from Lee and Seo: generate distinct equal-area grid figures, devise ways to measure marble dispersion, identify properties of water shapes in a tilted prism, and identify geometric shapes sharing properties with a target shape. Participants were asked for multiple solutions; a separate number-pyramid creativity task measured baseline performance (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Table 3 and MCT).
task.duration: The experiment lasted 72 minutes (SD = 7) in the experimental group and 60 minutes (SD = 5) in the control group; task-only duration is not separately reported (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Procedure).

outcomes.name: MCT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rarity-based score assigned from human-coded answer categories. The proportion of each category among total responses determined its score: the reported frequency ranges 0-1%, 1-2%, and 2-3% received 3, 2, and 1 points, respectively. A participant’s category scores were summed, with each category counted once within a task. This is a fixed frequency rubric, not a holistic creativity rating; the reference pool for category frequencies is not explicitly defined. Two scorers independently scored all solutions and resolved discrepancies; their qualifications and blinding are not stated. Scores were summed across the four tasks for each participant (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring). The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience are analyses of this same outcome, not separate outcomes (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50, Results).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 4.82, SD = 2.64 (analyzed n = 60); control M = 3.78, SD = 2.29 (analyzed n = 64); t(122) = 2.34, d = 0.42, p = 0.021 (Table 5). ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 5.44, η²p = 0.04, p = 0.021 (Results, H1a-c).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Table 5; PDF pp. 11-12 (printed pp. 49-50), Results, H1a-c, for ANCOVA; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, and PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2, for analyzed counts.

outcomes.name: MCT flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct answer categories represented in a participant’s correct solutions, summed across the tasks. Categories were coded manually; this is variety within one person’s solutions, not diversity across people. Two scorers independently scored all solutions and resolved discrepancies; their qualifications and blinding are not stated. Scores were summed across the four tasks for each participant (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring). The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience are analyses of this same outcome, not separate outcomes (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50, Results).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 15.12, SD = 3.71 (analyzed n = 60); control M = 12.50, SD = 3.49 (analyzed n = 64); t(122) = 4.05, d = 0.73, p = 0.000 (Table 5, as printed). ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 16.60, η²p = 0.12, p < 0.001 (Results, H1a-c).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Table 5; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for group counts; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2, for analyzed sample; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Results, H1a-c, for ANCOVA.

outcomes.name: MCT fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of correct answers in each category, with a maximum of 5 points as stated in the scoring rubric, summed over categories and tasks. Incorrect solutions were identified before scoring. Two scorers independently scored all solutions and resolved discrepancies; their qualifications and blinding are not stated. Scores were summed across the four tasks for each participant (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring). The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience are analyses of this same outcome, not separate outcomes (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50, Results).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 29.25, SD = 8.65 (analyzed n = 60); control M = 23.73, SD = 8.08 (analyzed n = 64); t(122) = 3.67, d = 0.66, p = 0.000 (Table 5, as printed). ANCOVA controlling prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 13.90, η²p = 0.10, p < 0.001 (Results, H1a-c).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Table 5; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for group counts; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2, for analyzed sample; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Results, H1a-c, for ANCOVA.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Not stated. The paper describes recruitment for this study and does not identify a shared sample or reanalysis of another paper’s participants.
sample_overlap.quote: The corresponding author coordinated with counsellors to recruit students from all majors and announced the topic of the study (“Mathematical Creativity Tasks”).

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is disclosed. Author affiliations are at Yangzhou University; the funding statement lists Chinese public, university, teaching-reform, and academic talent-support programmes. ChatGPT is the intervention tool.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 39), affiliations; PDF p. 18 (printed p. 56), Funding.

eligibility.reason: The explicit statement that students were randomly assigned to ChatGPT or no ChatGPT meets criterion 1 despite the quasi-experimental title (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure). This was a controlled classroom experiment with recruited volunteers, coded lab_rct rather than ordinary-coursework field research (same locator; PDF p. 17, printed p. 55, Limitations). The analyzed sample was 124 people, with 60 experimental and 64 control participants, exceeding the threshold of 50 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants and Table 2). Actual solutions to open-ended tasks were independently scored for originality, flexibility, and fluency (PDF pp. 8-10, printed pp. 46-48, MCT and Mathematical creativity scoring). ChatGPT was available while experimental-group solutions were produced, so these are with_ai outcomes (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 43-44, Procedure and Figures 1-2).

one_line_finding: The ChatGPT group scored higher than controls on flexibility (d = 0.73), fluency (d = 0.66), and originality (d = 0.42) in mathematical creativity tasks (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5).
open_questions: What randomization procedure was used? The title and abstract call the study quasi-experimental, while Procedure explicitly states random assignment (PDF pp. 1 and 4, printed pp. 39 and 42).

How many people were initially randomized and how many withdrew in each arm? Withdrawals are mentioned without counts, and Figure 1 does not separate initial assignment from retained participants (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 42-43).

Were originality-category frequencies computed over the pooled sample or separately within each arm? The rarity-scoring reference pool is not explicitly defined (PDF p. 9, printed p. 47, Mathematical creativity scoring).
notes: The entire markdown was read through the references and final citation; the PDF has no appended supplement, and no supplement, preregistration, data repository, or code repository is identified. Locators give PDF page positions and printed journal page numbers. Figure 1 group counts and the Figure 2 model label were checked visually after extracting page text because the figures are raster images. Author names and order follow the document, including Gang Li. The three post-intervention creativity indicators are the relevant scored-output outcomes; none is explicitly designated primary. The baseline creativity task precedes the intervention and is not after_ai; self-efficacy, self-evaluation, metacognitive bias indices, interest, difficulty, mental effort, and perceived ChatGPT usefulness are not coded as output creativity/diversity outcomes (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1; PDF pp. 8-12, printed pp. 46-50, Measures and Results). No unassisted post-AI creative task or between-person diversity outcome is reported. Table 5 states that its p values were Benjamini-Hochberg corrected; Data analysis says ANCOVA p values were similarly corrected (PDF pp. 8 and 11, printed pp. 46 and 49). Printed d, F, partial eta-squared, and p values are retained without recalculation, including p = 0.000; no standard errors or confidence intervals are reported for these creativity contrasts. The ChatGPT intervention also included structured prompts absent from the control, which the authors acknowledge limits isolation of the AI effect (PDF p. 14, printed p. 52, Discussion). Experimental sessions were longer, and the authors identify additional time as a possible contributor (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Procedure; PDF p. 17, printed p. 55, Limitations). Procedure inconsistently permits browsing on PDF p. 5 but prohibits external resources on PDF p. 6; it explicitly says no experimental participant chose to browse.
